title: Where each token sits
objectives: Explain why attention needs positions, and add learned or sinusoidal position vectors.

screens.title: Two orders, one answer
screens.prose: Take lesson 10's trained model and leave out its position table. Feed it ".mar" and ".amr": the last symbol is r in both, and the earlier symbols are the same set in a different order. The bars are the chance it gives to i as the next letter.

state.caption: Positions left out: the two chances are equal.

frames.caption: Positions left out: the two chances are equal.

screens.question: With positions left out, by how much do the two chances of i differ?

hints.text: Read the two bars with positions out.
The last position attends to the same set of tokens in both.
A weighted average over a set does not depend on its order.

feedback.correct: They are equal, 0.2377 each: without positions the model cannot tell the orders apart.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the two bars with positions out.

byKey.withpos: That is the gap with positions in. Switch them out.

explain.text: Without positions the last query is r in both and it averages over the same set $\{., m, a, r\}$, so the chances match: 0.2377. With positions they become 0.2910 and 0.4306. (The mask itself carries some order: earlier positions see fewer tokens.)

screens.title: Adding a position vector
screens.prose: Attention is blind to order, so add a **position vector** to each token's embedding before the first layer. It is either **learned**, a table with one row per position as in the supplied model, or **sinusoidal**: $PE_{t, 2i} = \sin(t/10000^{2i/d})$ and $PE_{t, 2i+1} = \cos(t/10000^{2i/d})$, from $t = 0$. Take $d = 32$.
screens.question: What is $PE_{3, 0}$? Give 4 decimal places.

byKey.deg: You took 3 degrees. The angle is 3 radians.

explain.text: $PE_{3,0} = \sin(3) = 0.1411$ and $PE_{3,1} = \cos 3 = -0.9900$. Low dimensions swing fast with $t$, higher ones slowly, like the hands of a clock.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide 5 by 1.7783, then take the sine.

byKey.i2: You used $i = 2$. Entry 2 is the sine with $i = 1$.

explain.text: The angle is $5/1.7783 = 2.8117$, so $PE_{5,2} = 0.3239$ and $PE_{5,3} = -0.9461$. Every position gets a unique pattern, computed, not learned.

screens.title: Offsets, not places
screens.prose: Take the dot product of two sinusoidal position vectors $t$ and $t + k$. Each sine and cosine pair gives $\cos(k\,\omega_i)$, so the sum depends on the offset $k$ alone, not on $t$. The curve is that sum for $d = 32$ against $k$.
screens.question: What is the dot product of a position vector with itself ($k = 0$)?

feedback.correct: $d/2 = 16$; at $k = 1$ it is 15.31, and it falls away as $k$ grows.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the sine and cosine pairs.

explain.text: $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$ for each of the 16 pairs, so the self dot product is 16 at every $t$; at offset 1 it is 15.31. $\mathbf p_{t+k}$ is a fixed rotation of $\mathbf p_t$ for every $t$, which Vaswani et al. expected to make "look 3 back" easy to learn.

screens.title: Beyond the trained context
screens.prose: The supplied model has a learned table of 8 rows, one per position. A sinusoidal table can be computed for any $t$.
screens.question: A sequence of 12 tokens arrives. What happens?

options.text: The learned table has no rows 8 to 11; the sinusoidal one has them, though whether the model uses them well is untested
Both work equally well, since positions are just numbers
options.why: A learned table simply has no row for position 9: the lookup fails.

options.text: Neither can be used past 8
options.why: Sinusoidal vectors exist for every $t$; the question is only how well a model trained to 8 uses them.

hints.text: A learned table has one trained row per position seen.
A formula has a value at every $t$.

feedback.correct: Learned rows end at the trained context; the formula never ends, but the model never practised there.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare a table with a formula.

explain.text: Learned positions cannot reach past the trained context: there is no row to look up. Sinusoidal ones can be computed for any $t$, which is part of why Vaswani et al. chose them; extrapolating well is a separate question.

screens.title: Concatenating instead of adding
screens.prose: A colleague joins the position vectors to the embeddings side by side, `np.concatenate([E, P], axis=1)`, for embeddings of width 32 feeding a layer whose $\mathbf W_Q$ is 32 by 32.
screens.question: What happens at the first layer?

options.text: The input is now 64 wide, so the product with the 32 by 32 matrices fails
It works the same as adding
options.why: Concatenating doubles the width; the weights expect 32.

options.text: It works if the positions are added after attention instead
options.why: Adding after attention is too late: the scores, where order matters, were already computed without them.

hints.text: A $T \times 64$ times $32 \times 32$ product does not exist.

feedback.correct: Shapes break: the model expects positions added.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What width comes out of the concatenation?

byKey.after: Positions added after attention arrive once the scores are fixed, so attention stays blind to order.

explain.text: The standard transformer adds position vectors to the embeddings, keeping the width. Concatenating needs wider weights; adding positions after attention leaves the scores blind to order.

screens.title: An index past the table
screens.prose: Edge case: `add_positions(E, P)` adds `P[:T]` to embeddings `E` of $T$ rows. With the learned table of 8 rows and $T = 10$, a careful version raises an error instead of silently adding a shorter table.
screens.question: Which error should it raise?

options.text: `IndexError`: there is no row for positions 8 and 9
None: NumPy broadcasts the 8 rows
options.why: Shapes $(10, 32)$ and $(8, 32)$ do not broadcast; and silently padding would hide the bug.

options.text: `ZeroDivisionError`
options.why: Nothing is divided. The fault is a missing row.

hints.text: Asking for row 8 is an index out of range.

feedback.correct: An `IndexError`, so the caller learns the context is too long.

explain.text: A learned table indexed past its end must fail loudly: an `IndexError` naming the context length. The code screen tests for exactly that.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np


def sinusoidal_positions(T, d):
    P = np.zeros((T, d))
    t = np.arange(T)[:, None]
    w = 1.0 / 10000 ** (np.arange(0, d, 2) / d)
    P[:, 0::2] = np.sin(t * w)
    P[:, 1::2] = np.cos(t * w)
    return P


def add_positions(E, P):
    E, P = np.asarray(E, dtype=float), np.asarray(P, dtype=float)
    if len(E) > len(P):
        raise IndexError(f'context {len(E)} is longer than the position table ({len(P)})')
    return E + P[:len(E)]


def order_matters(model, a, b):
    no = float(np.abs(last_logits(model, a) - last_logits(model, b)).max())
    yes = float(np.abs(last_logits(model, a, model['P']) - last_logits(model, b, model['P'])).max())
    return [no, yes]
widget.prelude:
import json
import numpy as np

with open('sequence-attn-names.json') as f:
    _W = json.load(f)
MODEL = {k: np.array(v) for k, v in _W['h1'].items()}
IX = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(_W['vocab'])}


def last_logits(model, tokens, P=None):
    X = np.asarray(tokens)
    T = len(X)
    x = model['E'][X] + (P[:T] if P is not None else 0.0)
    q, k, v = x @ model['Wq'], x @ model['Wk'], x @ model['Wv']
    S = q @ k.T / np.sqrt(q.shape[-1]) + np.triu(np.full((T, T), -np.inf), 1)
    S = S - S.max(-1, keepdims=True)
    A = np.exp(S)
    A = A / A.sum(-1, keepdims=True)
    return ((A @ v) @ model['Wo'] @ model['U'] + model['c'])[-1]

screens.title: Where each token sits
screens.prose:
Attention needs order supplied from outside:
$$\mathbf x_t = \mathbf e_{\text{token}_t} + \mathbf p_t, \qquad p_{t,2i} = \sin\!\big(t/10000^{2i/d}\big),\; p_{t,2i+1} = \cos\!\big(t/10000^{2i/d}\big),$$
or $\mathbf p_t$ a learned row of a table. Sinusoidal dot products depend on the offset only.
screens.question: Why add rather than concatenate?

options.text: Adding keeps the width, so every later weight keeps its shape
Adding keeps more information than concatenating
options.why: Concatenating keeps both intact; adding mixes them. The reason is the width.

options.text: Adding makes attention faster
options.why: Both cost about the same; the point is the shape.

feedback.correct: Same width, so the model is unchanged; it learns to read both from one vector.

explain.text: Adding keeps $\mathbf x_t$ at width $d$, and in high dimensions the model can still separate the token and position parts. Concatenating would need every weight matrix widened.

screens.title: Day of the week, days to earnings
screens.prose: A transformer reads 60 days of a stock's returns. Mondays behave differently, and returns are wilder in the days before an earnings date. Each day's return is embedded as a vector.
screens.question: How does the model learn about weekdays and earnings?

options.text: Add vectors for the weekday and the days to earnings, as position vectors are added
It reads them from the order of the days automatically
options.why: Attention without positions cannot see order at all, let alone weekdays.

options.text: Through the causal mask
options.why: The mask hides the future; it says nothing about which day is a Monday.

hints.text: Order and calendar facts must be written into them.
Add learned vectors for each weekday and each distance.

feedback.correct: Positions generalise to any fact about where a token sits.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What can attention see?

explain.text: Attention mixes vectors and sees nothing else. Position, weekday and distance to earnings are all "where this token sits", and each is written in by adding a vector before the first layer.

ideas: Without positions, attention averages over a set: ".mar" and ".amr" get the same chance of i next, 0.2377, until positions are added.
Add a position vector to each embedding: learned rows, or sinusoids $\sin(t/10000^{2i/d})$ and $\cos(\cdot)$; $PE_{3,0} = 0.1411$. Their dot products depend on the offset only.
Learned tables stop at the trained context (index past it and fail); sinusoids extend to any $t$. Add positions to the embeddings, before attention, never concatenated or after.
summary.trap: Concatenating positions breaks the shapes; adding them after attention leaves the scores blind to order.
